headline: High-risk shared git/workspace and broad egress create default data-leak and conflict exposure; prompt-injection risk is lower but present via file-based handoff.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and writes git-tracked files and has no self-isolation; oh-my-openagent can ingest project files, runtime-injected MCPs, and hooks. That creates a file-based instruction bridge where Aider’s output can be treated as content by B. The interaction is plausible in default workflows, though not proven by direct evidence.
conditions: IF Aider writes attacker-controlled text into tracked files that oh-my-openagent later parses as instructions
IF oh-my-openagent enables hooks or MCPs that consume repository content without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic instruction parsing from repo files
Require explicit allowlists for hook-triggered actions
Separate review and execution workspaces
Add provenance tags to file-derived prompts
requires-engineering: enforce content-safety filters on shared files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code, git history, and model-provider API keys, while oh-my-openagent touches project code, AGENTS.md, README.md, session history, and provider auth data. Both have broad network egress and shared file access patterns, so sensitive code or secrets can flow from one agent into the other’s outputs or upstream APIs by default. The blast radius includes exfiltration.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or home-directory workspace
IF either agent forwards file contents or session context to external model providers or APIs
mitigations: Use separate OS users or containers
Remove secrets from shared workspaces
Restrict outbound network destinations
Mount read-only copies of sensitive repos
requires-engineering: add per-agent data-loss-prevention controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; oh-my-openagent has full-permissions mode, broad egress, browser execution, subprocesses, and runtime-injected MCPs/hooks. Both can mutate shared resources, and Aider explicitly shares state via a shared git repo. Without locking, concurrent writes and git-state races are likely and can corrupt work or overwrite changes.
conditions: IF both agents target the same git repository or overlapping files
IF oh-my-openagent runs in full-permissions mode while Aider auto-commits changes
mitigations: Serialize edits through one agent at a time
Use branch-per-agent workflows
Enable git locks or pre-commit conflict checks
Limit one agent to read-only access
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider produces code edits and git commits that oh-my-openagent can ingest from project files, AGENTS.md, or session history. Because B has browser, MCP, and task tools, it may act on A’s output without a strong verification boundary. The pathway exists in default workflows, but B is not documented as blindly authoritative, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF oh-my-openagent uses Aider-generated files as authoritative task context
IF B executes tasks or browser actions based on unverified code or instructions from A
mitigations: Require human review before execution
Add a verification step for Aider-generated outputs
Separate generation and action agents
Mark machine-generated files clearly
requires-engineering: add provenance-aware task gating

E_compliance.rationale: Aider handles model-provider API keys and git history; oh-my-openagent handles provider auth data, session history, and telemetry. The pair therefore concentrates sensitive operational data under two open-source agents with different retention and logging surfaces. No specific residency or certification mismatch is documented, so the risk is a policy mismatch rather than a proven breach.
conditions: IF either agent logs session history or auth prompts beyond the operator’s retention policy
IF provider or telemetry data is processed under a stricter residency or deletion requirement
mitigations: Disable telemetry where possible
Rotate provider keys regularly
Review retention settings for both agents
Keep regulated data out of shared sessions
requires-engineering: align logging and deletion policies across both agents
